ev.sibling_born.text.1: Your mother gave birth to another child. The house got more crowded, and louder.
ev.sibling_born.title.2: A New Voice in the House
ev.sibling_born.text.2: In the night a thin, unfamiliar cry woke you. In the morning your mother showed you a bundle: "There, now there are more of you." The bundle scrunched up its face and yelled again.
ev.sibling_born.text.3: Since morning the house has been full of neighbour women bringing swaddling cloths, food and advice. Your mother lies pale and happy, and a new baby squeaks in the cradle.
ev.sibling_born.text.4: The baby was born in a downpour, to the drumming of rain on the roof. Now everyone sleeps by the hearth, packed like puppies in a basket, and you got the spot right against the wall.
ev.sibling_born.text.5: "You're the big one now," your mother said, and let you hold the baby. It was heavier than you expected and smelled of milk.
ev.sibling_born.text.6: At night your mother sings the old lullaby she once sang to you. Only now it's over a new cradle, and you listen, pretending to be asleep.
ev.sibling_born.text.7: They sent you outside, and you sat on the doorstep half the day listening to the midwife bustle about indoors. Then the door opened and you were called in to meet someone.
ev.sibling_born.text.8: You studied the new baby for a long time: tiny fingers, a cross red face. "It can't do anything," you reported to your mother. She laughed: once, neither could you.
ev.sibling_born.text.9: Your old cradle was dragged out of the corner, shaken free of dust and made up fresh. Now the new baby sleeps in it, and somehow that stings.
ev.sibling_born.text.10: The new baby was given a name, and the house held a feast for it: guests, songs, sweets. You got more than anyone — while no one was looking.
ev.sibling_born.text.11: The baby screams at night loud enough to wake the whole street. Your mother paces from corner to corner with it, and you lie awake wondering when it will learn to be quiet.
ev.sibling_born.text.12: Now you have a new job: rocking the cradle while your mother cooks. You rock so hard that the baby falls asleep — and so do you.
ev.sibling_born.text.13: The baby came early, tiny as a kitten. Everyone in the house tiptoes about, and every morning the first thing you do is check that it's breathing.
ev.sibling_born.text.14: Over the new baby's cradle hang knotted charms, beads and red threads to keep harm away. Your mother told you not to touch them — but you secretly added a pebble of your own, for luck.
ev.sibling_born.text.15: The baby was born at dawn, while the house was asleep — all but your mother and the old midwife. Its cry woke you, and you thought it was a bird.
ev.sibling_born.text.16: There's one more mouth in the house now. You jealously make sure the baby isn't getting your porridge — even though it only drinks milk so far.
ev.brawl.text.1: Some bully insulted you and your family in front of everyone.
ev.brawl.text.2: At the well a hulking lout shoved you away from the bucket and asked loudly, for the whole queue to hear, whether all your kin were thieves.
ev.brawl.text.3: Someone tripped you and you sprawled in the dust in the middle of the street. A grinning young man stands over you with his friends: "Watch your feet, bumpkin."
ev.brawl.text.4: In the eating house a drunken brute took your seat and swept your bowl onto the floor. The whole room has gone quiet, waiting to see what you'll do.
ev.brawl.text.5: A young man from the next farm declared in front of everyone that your family secretly moved the boundary stone, and spat at your feet.
ev.brawl.text.6: In the festival crush some bully dumped broth over you and announced loudly that it was an improvement.
ev.brawl.text.7: A gang of idlers at the gate has been mimicking your walk and accent for days. Today their leader blocked your way.
ev.brawl.text.8: A trader cheated you on the weights, and when you noticed he bellowed down the whole row that you're a thief from a family of thieves.
ev.brawl.text.9: On a narrow bridge a big man comes straight at you with no intention of giving way. "Step aside, nobody," he says loudly, so everyone can hear. "Your place is in the ditch."
ev.brawl.text.10: You learned that a young man from your street has been telling vile stories about you. Right now he's in the middle of the square repeating them, looking you straight in the eye.
ev.brawl.text.11: At the bank where everyone draws water, a stranger's labourer pushed in ahead, and when you objected he said people like you can wait till tomorrow. People around are snickering.
ev.brawl.text.12: A pebble hit you in the back. You turned to see a bully not even bothering to hide: "Well? What are you going to do about it?"
ev.brawl.text.13: A tipsy guest at someone's wedding loudly compared you to a scarecrow, and half the table roared with laughter.
ev.brawl.text.14: A big man with a stick demands you hand over what you're carrying — "toll for walking our street." Passers-by look away.
ev.brawl.text.15: While you were busy, someone smeared mud on your doorstep and scratched a lewd drawing beside it. The joker isn't even hiding — he's grinning on the corner.
ev.brawl.text.16: An out-of-town youth at the market gate announced loudly that your whole district is cowards and simpletons — and jabbed a finger at you: "Take this one, for instance."
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.1: You can already tell from his footsteps how much your father has drunk. Tonight they are heavy and uneven, and {npc} is looking for someone to take it out on before he's even through the door.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.2: Your father came back from the feast near dawn, singing and stumbling. The song broke off at the threshold: {npc} saw you and scowled, as if you were to blame for something.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.3: Your father wasn't paid for his work, and {npc} spent all evening at a friend's with a jug. Now he's home, and every word anyone says sounds wrong to him.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.4: A clay bowl smashed against the wall — {npc} didn't like the stew. Your father has been drunk since noon, and you know the next thing thrown won't be a bowl.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.5: Your father isn't shouting. {npc} sits in the dark, staring silently at the door, an empty jug beside him. This silence is worse than any shouting.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.6: Your father and his cronies are carousing in the yard: laughter, songs, banging cups. Then the cronies leave, and {npc} comes inside looking for whoever looked at him wrong.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.7: Only this morning {npc} swore not another drop. By evening your father can barely stand, and he demands you admit you blabbed everything to the neighbours.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.8: On his way back from work, {npc} stopped where they brew strong drink and came home after dark. The dog has crawled under the shed — it knows those footsteps too.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.roam.ok.8: You sat out past the last houses until dawn, listening to the frogs and distant dogs. The fields at night are frightening, but no more than home.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.9: Your father brought guests home and ordered food served, though the larder was empty. The guests have gone, and {npc}, drunk and furious, is looking for someone to blame for his shame.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.10: In the middle of the night someone hammered on the door: {npc} couldn't get into his own house. You opened it — and your father lurched in, breathing drink and curses all over you.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.11: At noon {npc} took your first earnings — "for the household." By night your father is back, drunk and penniless, demanding from the doorway where you're hiding the rest.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.12: Your father came back from his old friend's wake and can't stop: he drinks and weeps, then suddenly starts shouting. {npc} doesn't know himself who he's angry at.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.13: {npc} has drunk away the savings meant for hard times again. Your father sits by the cold hearth muttering that it's all someone else's fault — then lifts a heavy gaze to you.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.14: Your father went to the fair to sell a month's work and came back without the goods, without the money, and merry. The merriment ended at the threshold: {npc} is looking for someone to take it out on.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.15: You broke a jug — a small thing; on a sober day your father would only grumble. But {npc} has been drinking since morning, and you hear him slowly getting up from the bench.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.text.16: Rain lashes the walls, and the house smells of drink and anger. {npc} has already slammed his fist on the table twice, and your father seems to be just getting started.
ev.v_rel_father_drunk.roam.ok.16: You sat under someone's awning until dawn, soaked to the skin. Cold — but home would have been worse.
ev.c_h_aging.text.4: A boy at the well offered to carry your load — "it must be heavy for you." You refused, carried it yourself, and spent half the evening rubbing your lower back.
ev.c_h_aging.text.5: The climb to your house, which you once took in a single breath, now needs two stops. You pretend you're admiring the view.
ev.c_h_aging.text.6: You caught your reflection in the water and didn't recognize it at once: who is this tired person with lines around the eyes?
ev.c_h_aging.text.7: Your knees now forecast rain better than any soothsayer. The neighbours drop by to ask whether it's worth hanging out the washing today.
ev.c_h_aging.text.8: Twice this morning you forgot where you'd put the knife — and both times it was in your hand.
ev.c_h_aging.text.9: You used to sleep like a log until dawn. Now you wake in the dark and listen to everyone else sleeping.
ev.c_h_aging.text.10: You bit into a hard crust, and the tooth that had served you faithfully stayed behind in it. Now you chew on the other side.
ev.c_h_aging.text.11: The young folk sing some new songs, and you catch yourself thinking the old songs were better. That's exactly what the old people said when you were a child.
ev.c_h_aging.text.12: In the mornings your fingers won't bend until you've warmed them over the fire. The work gets done, but slower than you'd like.
ev.c_h_aging.text.13: You lifted a sack the way you had all your life — and something crunched in your back. For three days you walked like an old heron.
ev.c_h_aging.text.14: These days you have to ask people in the far corner to repeat themselves. On the bright side, you no longer hear half the nonsense.
ev.c_h_aging.text.15: Your feet get cold at night now, even in warm weather. You've acquired an extra blanket and are no longer embarrassed about it.
ev.c_h_aging.text.16: At the festival dance you lasted exactly one round. There was a time when you were the last to be dragged off the square.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.1: {npc} dragged home a stray puppy and swears it will guard the house. So far it is diligently guarding only your shoe — and has already chewed through half of it.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.1.E03: {npc} dragged home a stray puppy and swears it will guard the house. So far it is diligently guarding only your sandal — and has already chewed through half of it.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.2: {npc} picked up a fledgling that fell out of its nest and feeds it soaked grain from a fingertip. The chick screams from dawn demanding more, and now the whole house gets up with it.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.3: {npc} brought a turtle home from the stream and announced it would live in the house. For now it lives under your bed, and you've stepped on it twice in one night.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.4: There's a frog in the water jar. {npc} insists it's {g=npc_sex:his|her} best friend and understands every word. Now the water has to go in a different jar.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.5: {npc} nursed a crow with a broken wing. The wing has healed, but the crow won't leave: it sits on the roof, steals anything shiny and wakes the house with its hoarse cawing.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.6: {npc} has tamed a lizard — or so {g=npc_sex:he|she} believes. It basks on the doorstep and vanishes whenever you come near, and {npc} takes offence on its behalf every time.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.7: A mangy dog followed {npc} all the way home from the market, and {g=npc_sex:he|she} begged to keep it. The dog ate a dinner nobody offered it and lay down by the door as if it had always lived there.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.8: {npc} caught a cricket and put it in a little woven cage by the bed. Now the cricket sings all night, and {npc} sleeps like a log — unlike you.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.9: {npc} brought home a live little fish in a pot and forbade anyone to eat it. The fish is called Queenie and gets crumbs from the family table every day.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.10: {npc} brought home a duckling that had lost its brood. Now the duckling follows its rescuer everywhere — even to the privy.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.11: {npc} keeps a tame mouse inside {g=npc_sex:his|her} shirt and feeds it crumbs. You found out when it poked its nose out in the middle of dinner, in front of guests.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.12: {npc} has built a pen for snails in the yard — there are already twenty, each with a name. Meanwhile the snails are steadily making for your pots of herbs.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.13: {npc} traded {g=npc_sex:his|her} best pebble and a leather strap to the kids next door for a puppy. The puppy has proved a great connoisseur of your belongings: it has already made off with the broom and your belt.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.14: {npc} carries a huge beetle around in cupped hands, showing everyone how it waves its feelers. The beetle lives in a box by the bed, and at night you can hear it scratching.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.15: {npc} found an owlet in a hollow tree and dragged it home "to warm it up." It stares at everyone with round eyes, clacks its beak, and has already begged a piece of meat from the pot.
ev.a_child_puppy.text.16: {npc} brought a baby hare in from the fields and hid it in the laundry basket. The leveret has gnawed through the basket and half the washing, and seems perfectly content.
ev.f_charity.text.1: The time has come to give your due to the poor and the temple. The neighbours know how much you have, and they are watching to see how much you give.
ev.f_charity.text.1.islamic: It is time to pay the zakat — a fortieth of your savings, for the poor and the needy. It is not a kindness but a duty: wealth is purified when it is shared.
ev.f_charity.text.1.christian: The church is collecting its tithe, and beggars sit at the church gates. A neighbour has already boasted of how much he gave.
ev.f_charity.text.1.jewish: The community's collector goes from house to house: for the poor, for widows, for ransoming captives. Everyone has their share.
ev.f_charity.text.1.dharmic: It is the season of offerings: generosity is the first of virtues, and every gift, they say, returns in this life or the next. The monks and the temple are waiting.
ev.f_charity.text.2: An elder stands at your gate with a basket: they're collecting for the poor before the great festival. He reads out loud who gave what — and waits to hear from you.
ev.f_charity.text.3: A dozen houses burned in the lower quarter, and the families who lost everything are sleeping by the shrine. Its keepers are going round the well-off: everyone must help as they can.
ev.f_charity.text.4: An old beggar has sat on your doorstep for three days, silently watching goods being carried into your house. The neighbours are asking how long you'll pretend not to see him.
ev.f_charity.text.5: The harvest was thin, and by the end of the season many in the district have empty stores. The elders are collecting grain and goods for the hungry — and they came to you first.
ev.f_charity.text.6: Long ago you vowed that if things went well you'd share with the poor. Things went well. And it seems heaven isn't the only one that remembers — so does the whole street.
ev.f_charity.text.7: Orphans live at the shrine, and by custom the well-off feed them on the feast day. This year it's your turn, and the attendant is already bringing out the empty bowls.
ev.f_charity.text.8: The roof of the house of prayer is leaking, and the community is collecting for repairs. Everyone gives according to their means — and everyone knows yours.
ev.f_charity.text.9: A widow in your quarter is left with three children and nothing to eat. The holy man who visits the quarter asked the gathering loudly: who will help?
ev.f_charity.text.10: Pilgrims are passing through your district — on foot, barefoot, with staffs. By custom every household gives them bread and something for the road, and the richest give the most.
ev.f_charity.text.11: The harvest festival has come: the first share goes to the shrine and the poor. Your neighbour is already carrying his — deliberately slowly, so everyone can see.
ev.f_charity.text.12: Sickness is going round the town, and a shelter for poor patients has been set up by the shrine. They need food, blankets and medicine, and the attendants are going door to door.
ev.f_charity.text.13: You dreamed of a beggar holding out his hand and woke with a heavy heart. And that very afternoon they came round collecting for the poor.
ev.f_charity.text.14: Bandits carried off people from a neighbouring village, and the community is gathering a ransom. A crier calls out the names of those who have already given.
ev.f_charity.text.15: A lonely old pauper has died, and there's nothing to pay for his last rites. The keeper of the shrine came to you: custom says everyone deserves a decent farewell.
ev.f_charity.text.16: Before the new year, custom says you give to the poor so the year will be generous. A queue has already formed at your gate, and the whole street is watching to see what you bring out.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.1: The neighbour who once started out level with you has bought a second house and now travels by litter. Every time you pass his gate, something burns under your ribs.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.2: The neighbour who until recently patched his roof with whatever came to hand has re-roofed his whole house and put up carved gates. You catch yourself counting every new beam.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.3: In a year the neighbour's herd has doubled, while yours is just as it was. Every morning his animals are driven past your gate, and every morning it's harder to bear.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.4: The neighbour threw a feast for the whole street: musicians, roast meat, more guests than you've had in your life. You were invited too — which somehow makes it worse.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.5: Hail flattened your field, yet seemed to skip the neighbour's right over the boundary. Now he's selling grain at three times the price — to you among others.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.6: The neighbour has been chosen headman of the quarter: people bow to him now and call on him to settle disputes. Not long ago you stood shoulder to shoulder grumbling about the old headman.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.7: At every festival the neighbour shows up in new clothes, and his household jingles with ornaments. You've worn the same holiday best for three years running.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.8: The neighbour bought for a song the very thing you turned down — and sold it for three times as much. Now when you meet he claps you on the shoulder: "Don't be so timid next time!"
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.9: The neighbour has hired hands now: they fetch water, sweep the yard, run his errands. You still do everything yourself and watch it all over the fence.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.10: A powerful patron has taken notice of the neighbour, and now important visitors keep stopping at his gate. No one knocks at yours except the tax collector.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.11: The neighbour tore down his old hut and is building a house twice the size — so big that in the evenings its shadow falls across your yard. The walls rise every day, and something rises inside you too.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.12: The neighbour dug a well of his own, while you still haul water from the common one. He kindly offered to let you draw from his — with a smile that made you wish he hadn't.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.13: Customers are queuing at the neighbour's door, though his hands, as you well know, are no better than yours. Passing by, you hear him whistling, and you grit your teeth.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.14: The neighbour, they say, dug up a pot of old treasure in his garden. Since then he's been strutting about, while you've dug up your whole yard and found nothing but potsherds.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.15: The neighbour is showing off his new things: dishes from distant lands, a rug, a patterned lamp. Yesterday he spent half an hour leading you round his house, and you nodded along, smiling through gritted teeth.
ev.v_envy_neighbor.text.16: You and the neighbour are the same age and have kept neck and neck all your lives. But this year he's lucky in everything and you in nothing, and at night you toss and turn thinking about his gate.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is afraid of the dark: the old woman next door told stories of a night creature that steals naughty children. Now a lamp burns by the bed all night, and the oil goes as if it were a festival.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.1.E03: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is afraid of the dark: the old woman next door told stories of Lamia, who steals naughty children. Now a lamp burns by the bed all night, and the oil goes as if it were a festival.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.2: {npc} insists something is breathing under the bed. You had to leave a light burning all night, and in the morning buy a charm against night spirits from the wise woman as well.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.3: Since the thunderstorm {npc} is afraid to fall asleep in the dark: what if the thunder comes back? The lamp burns till morning now, and {npc} only drops off holding your finger.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.4: {npc} heard stories from the street boys about the dead who walk at night. Now a light burns by the bed until dawn, and you keep getting up to top up the oil.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.5: {npc} woke up screaming: the shadow of the drying herbs on the wall had become a monster with long arms. You moved the herbs, but now the light burns till morning anyway.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.6: {npc} isn't afraid of the dark — only of you leaving the room. You had to buy a bigger lamp and promise to sit nearby until {g=npc_sex:he|she} falls asleep.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.7: At night {npc} heard an owl screech in the yard and decided it was calling {g=npc_sex:his|her} name. Now sleep is only possible with a light on and you singing.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.8: {npc} announced that a dark man lives in the corner and wouldn't go to bed until you'd gone round the whole house with a light. The patrol repeats every night, and oil isn't getting any cheaper.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.9: An old storyteller in the square told a frightening tale, and {npc} listened open-mouthed. Now a light burns by the bed every night, and you tell stories with happy endings.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.10: {npc} came to you in the middle of the night, trembling: "Something's rustling in there." It was a mouse, but proving it took a light — and the lamp has burned till morning ever since.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.11: To chase away {npc}'s night fears you bought an amulet "against all monsters at once" from a peddler. The amulet didn't help; the lamp did. Now you have both.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.12: The wind howls through the cracks, and {npc} is sure it's something terrible crying. You keep a light going at night and spend more on oil than you'd like.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.13: {npc} is afraid that in the night you'll vanish if your face can't be seen. Silly, of course — but you leave a light on and sleep facing {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.14: {npc} dreamed of a huge beast and is now afraid to close {g=npc_sex:his|her} eyes in the dark. You made {g=npc_sex:him|her} a wooden "beast-sword" and left the lamp burning.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.15: Every evening it's the same: "A little more light, one more story." {npc} only drops off around midnight, and the house goes through twice as much oil as before.
ev.c_fear_dark.text.16: {npc} refuses to sleep in the corner: there, {g=npc_sex:he|she} says, "the darkness is watching." You bought a new mat, laid it next to yours, and left a small light at the head of the bed.
ev.a_first_word.text.1: {npc} said {g=npc_sex:his|her} first word. It wasn't "mama" or "papa" but the name of the neighbors' dog — and you still told the whole street about it.
ev.a_first_word.text.2: {npc} said {g=npc_sex:his|her} first word: "give." Since then {g=npc_sex:he|she} has said it a hundred times a day and, it must be admitted, very persuasively.
ev.a_first_word.text.3: {npc} pointed at the hearth fire and said clearly: "Hot!" Evidently some lessons have already been learned the hard way.
ev.a_first_word.text.4: {npc} said {g=npc_sex:his|her} first word to a crow on the fence: "Shoo!" The crow didn't budge, but you laughed so hard the whole street came running to look.
ev.a_first_word.text.5: {npc} stayed silent for ages, just watching — and then came out with a whole "more porridge." You ran to tell the neighbours before the porridge got cold.
ev.a_first_word.text.6: {npc}'s first word was "no." It was delivered firmly and with dignity — and it looks set to remain a favourite for a long time.
ev.a_first_word.text.7: "Mama!" {npc} announced — while looking, for some reason, at the cooking pot. The pot said nothing, but you decided it was a good start all the same.
ev.a_first_word.text.8: {npc} said {g=npc_sex:his|her} first word in {g=npc_sex:his|her} sleep — something like "num-num." You lay awake till morning waiting for more, but there was no more.
ev.a_first_word.text.9: {npc}'s first word was your favourite curse. You don't remember saying it all that often, but the neighbours seem to.
ev.a_first_word.text.10: {npc} pointed at the moon and said "Lah!" Everyone agreed that meant "moon," and since then you go out together in the evenings to look at it.
ev.a_first_word.text.11: {npc}'s first word was "papa" — addressed to the neighbours' old dog. The dog took it with dignity; you took it with pride.
ev.a_first_word.text.12: {npc} copied the street vendor: "Fresh! Fresh!" — and has no plans to say anything else yet. But very loudly.
ev.a_first_word.text.13: {npc}'s first word was {g=npc_sex:his|her} own name, slightly wrong. Now the whole house calls {g=npc_sex:him|her} by the version {g=npc_sex:he|she} came up with.
ev.a_first_word.text.14: {npc}'s first word was "again!" as you tossed {g=npc_sex:him|her} up toward the ceiling. By evening your arms were falling off, but stopping was out of the question.
ev.a_first_word.text.15: {npc} said "drink" quietly — and you froze, jug in hand, afraid to scare the miracle away. You poured the water, of course, and spent the rest of the day telling everyone about it.
ev.a_first_word.text.16: {npc}'s first word was "baba" — and now that's what {g=npc_sex:he|she} calls everyone: neighbours, guests, even the tax collector. The tax collector seemed rather touched.
ev.c_toys.text.1: You made a little wooden horse on wheels. Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} pulls it around from dawn to dusk and feeds it barley — real barley, from your stores.
ev.c_toys.text.2: You sewed a rag doll with bead eyes. Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} puts it to bed, spoon-feeds it and scolds it sternly for misbehaving.
ev.c_toys.text.3: You made a rattle from a dried gourd with pebbles inside. {npc} shakes it from dawn to dusk, and now you always know exactly where {g=npc_sex:he|she} is.
ev.c_toys.text.4: You shaped a clay whistle like a little bird and fired it. {npc} blows it so rapturously that the neighbours' dogs answer in chorus.
ev.c_toys.text.5: You whittled a little boat with a rag sail. {npc} launches it in every puddle and comes home soaked to the ears and happy every time.
ev.c_toys.text.6: You rolled a ball from rags and wool and stitched leather round it. {npc} chases it round the yard, and you keep catching it just before it rolls into the hearth.
ev.c_toys.text.7: You carved a wooden spinning top. {npc} can't spin it yet but is ready to watch you do it until nightfall.
ev.c_toys.text.8: You modelled a whole herd out of clay: a dog, a bird, and something you claimed was a horse. {npc} recognized them all — even the horse, which counts as a triumph.
ev.c_toys.text.9: You fixed a carved horse's head with a fibre mane onto a stick. {npc} gallops round the yard on it, thundering like a whole herd.
ev.c_toys.text.10: You knocked together a little cart on wooden wheels. {npc} hauls stones and wood chips in it, and once a sleeping puppy from next door.
ev.c_toys.text.11: You wove a little man in a hat out of dry grass. {npc} named him {g=npc_sex:his|her} best friend, drags him everywhere and shares food with him.
ev.c_toys.text.12: You made a whirligig — a clay disc on a string that hums when you spin it. {npc} could twirl it for hours, and the whole house falls asleep to its hum.
ev.c_toys.text.13: You carved a wooden bird on wheels that flaps its wings when you pull it along. {npc} rolls it across the floor and flaps {g=npc_sex:his|her} arms back at it.
ev.c_toys.text.14: You made tiny pots: little bowls and a jug the size of a fingernail. {npc} cooks sand "stew" in them and serves the whole household, and you pretend to eat three helpings.
ev.c_toys.text.15: You hung a swing from a branch — a board on two ropes. {npc} swings from morning till night shouting "higher!" while you stand below, hand on your heart.
ev.c_toys.text.16: You strung painted beads and shells onto a cord. {npc} wears this treasure round {g=npc_sex:his|her} neck, won't take it off even at night, and shows it to every passer-by.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.1: The neighbor who has owed you for a whole year came empty-handed. You have every right to take his belongings in payment — but then his family will be begging.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.1.E03: The carter who has owed you for a whole year came empty-handed. You have every right to take his mules — but without the mules his family will be begging.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.2: The neighbour who borrowed from you for seed came without the money: hail stripped his field bare. His belongings would cover the debt — but then his family would have nothing to live on until the next harvest.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.2: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.2: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.3: The neighbour's storehouse burned down, and with it any hope of repaying you on time. He stands before you twisting his cap and offers you whatever is left himself.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.3: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.3: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.4: The neighbour lay in fever for half a year and couldn't work, while his debt to you kept growing. Now he can barely stand and begs you not to take his tools — without them he can't make a living.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.4: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.4: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.5: The neighbour's animals died, and the debt he meant to repay from their young can't be paid. By law his house and goods would go to you — and the whole street knows where he'd go then.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.5: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.5: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.6: The neighbour borrowed from you to trade in the next town but came back empty-handed: his goods were taken on the road. He swears he'll work it off — but the debt is large, and his belongings are right here.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.6: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.6: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.7: The tax collectors stripped the neighbour bare, and he can't repay you. He came himself — empty-handed, head bowed.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.7: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.7: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.8: The flood washed away the neighbour's garden and half his wall. He has owed you since last year and now asks you to wait — though for what, he doesn't know himself.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.8: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.8: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.9: A second bad harvest in a row — and the neighbour came without the money again. They say his household eats once a day, and you have every right to take the little that's left there.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.9: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.9: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.10: The neighbour, a craftsman, broke his arm and can't work for half a year, while his debt to you hangs over him. His tools are the only thing of value in the house, and you have every right to take them.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.10: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.10: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.11: A travelling trader swindled the neighbour, and the money set aside for you left with the swindler. The neighbour begs forgiveness, and behind him in the doorway stand his frightened children.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.11: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.11: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.12: The hungry year hit everyone, and the neighbour harder than most. He came to ask for more time, and you can see how thin he's grown these past months.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.12: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.12: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.13: The neighbour's pottery kiln cracked, and the whole batch was ruined in the firing. He can only repay you if he gets back on his feet — unless you take everything he owns right now.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.13: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.13: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.14: The neighbour always paid on time, but this time he came empty-handed and can't meet your eye. Taking his belongings is what anyone in your place would do, people say. Or almost anyone.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.14: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.14: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.15: The neighbour has seven mouths to feed and barely earns enough for bread. He's been unable to repay you for two years. Today he came and said quietly: "Take whatever you want."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.15: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.15: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.a_poor_debtor.text.16: Drought burned the crops, and the neighbour who promised to pay you after the harvest can't. He offers his plot of land in payment — the last thing feeding his family.
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.success.16: Two years later the neighbor paid everything in full — and a little extra "for your patience."
ev.a_poor_debtor.defer.failure.16: The extra time passed and there's still no money. Now the debtor crosses to the other side of the street.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.1: {g:An old wrestler who trains the young|An aging dancer who teaches the girls} looks you up and down: "Stooped shoulders, soft belly. Come to us — {g:running, wrestling, rubdowns|dancing, ball games, rubdowns}. In a year you won't recognize yourself."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.1.E03: {g:A trainer from the palaestra|The keeper of a bathhouse with an exercise yard} looks you up and down: "Stooped shoulders, soft belly. Come to us — {g:running, wrestling, oil and strigil|ball games, light weights and oil rubs}. In a year you won't recognize yourself."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.2: A grey-haired master of staff-fighting stopped you at his gate: "You walk like a sack of grain. Come mornings — staff, running, rubdowns. In half a year your back will thank you."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.2: The master snorted and went back into his yard. You watched him go and went off to lunch.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.3: Some acquaintances call you to the square where they play ball in the evenings: "We're one short! Twice a week — we chip in for the ground and the rubdowns." You look down at your belly and hesitate.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.3: They found another player, and you found an excuse for an early supper.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.4: The physician felt your pulse and shook his head: "Lazy heart, thick blood. Go to the trainer who teaches exercises — he doesn't charge much. Or at least walk more."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.4: The physician sighed: "Well, I've said my piece." You nodded and had a double helping that same evening.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.5: {g:At the festival you stepped into the wrestling ring and a moment later were flat on your back. The ring-master offered you a hand: "You've got strength, but no wind. Train with me — I'll make a wrestler of you."|At the festival you danced all evening, and next morning you couldn't get up. The dance teacher laughed: "You've got spirit, but no wind. Come to me — in a year you'll out-dance them all."}
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.5: {g:The ring-master|The teacher} shrugged: "Suit yourself." You trudged home, carefully nursing your aching sides.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.6: Every morning a group of people your age pass your house on their way to the river to swim and run along the bank. Yesterday one of them called out: "Come with us! We'll chip in for a trainer — and in a year you'll shed half yourself."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.6: They went to the river without you. You waved after them from the doorstep, a hot flatbread in hand.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.7: Archers gather by the town wall: they draw bows, run, haul stones. Their leader spotted you: "Your arms are strong; your belly isn't. Come along — the fee is small."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.7: The archer turned back to his target. You stood a while watching the arrows fly, then went about your business.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.8: An old pal you remember as plump suddenly turned up lean and lively: "I go to a trainer — running, stone-lifting, rubdowns. Come with me, it's dull on my own."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.8: Your pal waved and ran off — quite literally. You watched him go and went off to lunch.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.9: A wandering teacher is demonstrating exercises in the square: slow movements, deep breathing. He pointed at you: "You bend like a dry stick. Pay a little and you'll be supple as a young vine."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.9: The teacher shrugged and turned to the next onlooker. Your knees creaked as you headed home.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.10: At a feast you boasted that in your youth you outran everyone. A joker immediately offered: "Then come to our morning runs and wrestling. I'll pay your first month myself — if you last."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.10: The joker needled you all evening, but you were busy with the sweets.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.11: Your festival belt won't meet any more. A neighbour noticing your struggle suggested: "Go to the {g:wrestlers|dancers} across the river, they don't charge much. They've straightened out worse than you."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.11: You punched a new hole in the belt. Problem solved — for this year, at least.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.12: People from your quarter are training for the festival contests: running, tug-of-war, stone lifting. "Are you in? We practise every morning and chip in for a trainer."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.12: At the festival you cheered your side louder than anyone — from the bench, with a snack in hand.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.13: You were panting on the way uphill, and a young man running down the other way called out cheerfully: "Come run with us in the mornings! The master charges next to nothing for a month."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.13: The young man ran on downhill, and you sat on a rock to catch your breath. A good rock. Comfortable.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.14: They say the ruler himself exercises with trainers every morning, and now it's all the fashion. The {g:wrestling|dance} teacher in the square is calling to anyone who can pay: "In a year you'll be good as new!"
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.14: Fashions pass, you decided, but a belly stays. And off you went to lunch.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.15: You couldn't lift a basket you once carried one-handed, and {g:the old fist-fighter|the old dancer} from next door saw it. "Come to me," {g:he|she} said. "It's cheap, and it'll do you good."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.15: {g:The old fighter|The old dancer} just shook {g:his|her} head. You did get the basket home in the end — in two trips.
ev.c_h_gym_invite.text.16: At dawn a whole crowd is exercising in the square: stretching, running, wrestling. The trainer spotted you trudging sleepily past and shouted: "Hey! Same time tomorrow. And don't forget the fee."
ev.c_h_gym_invite.decline.ok.16: Same time next day you were fast asleep. The trainer didn't seem to mind.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.1: A messenger brings news: in a distant city a distant relative of yours has died childless — a man you never met. By his last wishes everything is yours: house, workshop, household. And debts, which no one can put a number to.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.1.E03: A messenger brings a sealed letter: in a distant city a distant relative of yours has died childless — a man you never met. His will leaves everything to you: house, workshop, slaves. And debts, which no one can put a number to.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.1.rome: A messenger brings a will sealed by seven witnesses: in a distant city a distant relative of yours has died childless. Everything is yours — on condition that you take his name and honor his tomb. And debts, which no one can put a number to.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.2: Word came: a distant uncle of yours has died — you saw him only once, as a child, at someone's wake. He had no children, so everything passes to you: house, workshop, storerooms. And along with it, who knows how many creditors.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.3: A stranger covered in road dust asked for you by name and handed you a signet ring: a distant kinsman of yours who traded in foreign lands has died without heirs. His warehouse and house are now yours — and so are all his unpaid debts.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.4: The headman of a hill village came to tell you that a lonely old man — a distant kinsman of yours — has died. His fields, orchards and house in the valley now pass to you. Only the neighbours whisper that the old man owed half the village.
The debts turned out to be trifles, and the land rich and well tended. Suddenly you're a person of means.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.5: You had no idea you had kin in the capital — until a court messenger arrived from there. A childless old man, a distant relative on your grandfather's side, has died and left you everything: a house by the market, a shop, storerooms. About the debts the messenger was evasive: "You'll sort it out."
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.6: Word came with some passing merchants: in a distant city a childless kinsman of your grandfather's has died, and by his last wishes everything passes to you. The merchants added that the house is a rich one — but creditors crowd its gate every day.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.7: A distant kinsman of yours has died — a famous master craftsman you never got round to apprenticing with. He had no children, and the workshop with all its tools and orders is now yours. Though they say he owed his customers more work than he ever finished.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.8: In the square a crier called out your name: you were being sought as an heir. A distant kinsman of yours, who died childless, has left you all his property — and, as is the way of things, all his debts, which have yet to be counted.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.9: A grey-haired old man who called himself the executor studied your face for a long time. Then he said: a distant kinsman of yours has died without children and left you everything — house, land, granaries. "And debts," he added. "How much, nobody knows."
The debts were small, and the land and granaries in perfect order. Suddenly you're a person of means.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.10: Beyond the mountains, in a city you've never set foot in, an old kinsman of your grandfather's has died childless. He left you a house, a shop, and a heap of unpaid debts that nobody has counted.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.11: You'd almost forgotten the old man who, when you were small, once gave you a honey cake and called you "his own blood." Now he has died, leaving no children — and by his wish his whole estate passes to you. Along with debts nobody has counted.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.12: The news arrived half a year late: a distant kinsman of yours, owner of an estate in the next province, has died. No other heirs could be found. The steward sends word that the household is in order — but creditors are already knocking at the gate.
The debts were small and the estate well run and profitable. Suddenly you're a person of means.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.13: A distant kinsman of yours has died — a moneylender the whole district cursed behind his back. He had no children, so it all comes to you: house, strongboxes and a pile of other people's debts. Though they say he had plenty of debts of his own.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.14: They said your great-uncle, who left home half a century ago, had long since perished. It turns out he grew rich in a distant city and died there childless, naming you his heir. House, workshop, household — and debts nobody knows a thing about.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.15: At night you dreamed of an unknown old man bowing silently. That afternoon a messenger came: a distant kinsman of yours has died childless and left you everything he had. Besides the house and goods there are debts — asked how large, the messenger only shrugged.
ev.t_distant_inheritance.text.16: You were summoned before the elders: in front of witnesses they declared the last wishes of a distant kinsman of yours who died childless. House, shop, stores — all yours. The elders exchanged glances: there are all sorts of rumours about the dead man's debts.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.1: The tooth has ached three nights running, your cheek is swollen, and you'd give anything to whoever makes it stop. There's a tooth-puller at the market, as it happens.
ev.c_h_tooth.title.2: A Feast with a Swollen Jaw
ev.c_h_tooth.text.2: You spent the whole feast in a corner clutching your cheek: the tooth shoots pain so sharp your vision goes dark. They say a tooth-puller with strong pincers is working the market square.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.3: You cracked a nut with your teeth — and a tooth cracked along with the shell. Now it responds to everything: hot, cold, even the wind. And as luck would have it, a tooth-puller is drumming up custom at the market.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.4: You haven't slept for two nights: the tooth aches as if an evil spirit had moved in. The neighbours advise herbs, or a charm, or the tooth-puller by the market gate.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.5: A travelling tooth-puller has come to the fair — with a drum to drown out the screams. And as if on cue, your back tooth has ached for a week and half your face is swollen.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.6: This morning you could barely open your mouth: your cheek is swollen as if you'd stuffed a whole bun in it. A neighbour took one look and said a single word: "Tooth-puller." He happens to be at the market.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.7: The tooth hurts so much your work keeps slipping out of your hands, and you can only eat thin porridge on one side of your mouth. They say the tooth-puller with his pincers is still at the market.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.8: In the middle of the night you shot up in bed, as if someone had pressed a hot coal into your jaw. You paced the house till morning, and at dawn you heard the tooth-puller calling for customers at the market.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.9: The wise woman gave you a bitter herb to chew, but the tooth only took offence and ached harder. Your cheek is swollen, and you're already glancing toward the market where the tooth-puller sits.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.10: You always loved honey and sweet things, and here's the price: a tooth has gone black and aches day and night. At the market a tooth-puller is showing the crowd a whole string of other people's teeth — to inspire confidence.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.11: The tooth flared up on the road, and by the time you reached the nearest town your cheek was swollen. Luckily there's a tooth-puller working in the square.
ev.c_h_tooth.pull.11: Off to the tooth-puller in the square
ev.c_h_tooth.pull.ok.11: Pincers, strong hands, one short howl — the onlookers in the square even applauded. The pain left with the tooth.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.12: One sip of cold water and you howled loud enough for the whole yard to hear. The bad tooth had been nagging for a while, but now there's no escaping the pain. The tooth-puller, they say, is at the market today.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.13: The tooth that's been wobbling since last year has suddenly flared up: the gum burns and your cheek has ballooned. The neighbours all say the same: go to the tooth-puller — he's at the market right now.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.14: Of course, right before an important day the tooth aches so badly you can neither talk nor eat. Across the square you can see the tooth-puller wiping his pincers.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.15: There was a stone in the bread, and the tooth split. Now half your face is one big ache, and there's a tooth-puller at the market, as you know. There's also fear.
ev.c_h_tooth.text.16: For five days you've rinsed with herbal brews, and the tooth only aches more. Even the dog seems to sigh sympathetically at your swollen cheek. Meanwhile, the tooth-puller is still at the market.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.1: For two years your partner has been doctoring the shared accounts. Under a floorboard you found the second, real record of accounts — and you didn't like the sum on it at all.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.1.E03: For two years your partner has been doctoring the shared accounts. Under a floorboard you found the second, real tablet of records — and you didn't like the sum on it at all.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.2: In the storehouse you share with your partner you counted the sacks — and there were fewer than he'd reported. The rest, it turns out, leave at night for a friend of his.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.3: A customer happened to mention the price he'd paid for your goods — twice what your partner had told you. For two years the difference has been settling in his purse.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.4: You checked the notches on your tally stick against what your partner had been reporting — and not a single month matched. He'd been cheating you a little at a time, but for a very, very long time.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.5: In your partner's shop you found a second set of weights — slightly lighter than the true ones. He'd been short-weighting customers, reporting modest takings to you and pocketing the difference.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.6: Your partner's clerk, having had too much at a festival, let it slip: the boss has long kept two sets of accounts — "one for himself and one for the suckers." The sucker, you quickly realised, was you.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.7: Your partner complains about a bad year — while building himself a new house. You dug through his records and found where the money comes from: your shared business.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.8: You opened a bale your partner was sending to a buyer — the goods inside were second-rate, and the good stuff, it turns out, he'd been selling on the side. Not a coin of it ever reached your shared purse.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.9: You walked in on your partner unannounced and saw him tucking a purse into a hole in the wall. Later you checked the hiding place: there was more in it than your business had made in two years.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.10: The supplier was surprised when you came in person: "But your partner always pays half of what he writes down." The difference, naturally, your partner kept.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.11: One night you noticed a light in the workshop and found your partner there altering the accounts, scraping out the old figures. In the morning you compared them — the difference had been piling up for years.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.12: An old worker who was leaving took you aside: "Check how much your partner actually charges the customers." You checked — and couldn't sleep half the night.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.13: A moneylender turned up demanding a debt you'd never heard of: your partner had borrowed against your shared business and stashed the money. You went through his records — and there it all was.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.14: Your partner in the shared fields complains of a poor harvest year after year. But you talked to his labourers and learned they brought in twice as much — and he sold the extra on the quiet.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.15: You saw your own seal on a deal you'd never made. Your partner, it turns out, had a copy made long ago — and has spent two years trading in your name for his own pocket.
ev.a_partner_cheat.text.16: Your partner left on business and forgot the key to his chest. Inside lay the real accounts — and the figures in them were very different from the ones he'd shown you.
ev.loan_request.text.1: A neighbor asks to borrow money: his wife is ill and the doctor is expensive.
ev.loan_request.text.2: A neighbour asks for a loan: lightning set his roof on fire, and he has to re-roof the house before the rains come.
ev.loan_request.text.3: A neighbour stands at your gate twisting his cap: the tax collector is threatening to take his house unless he pays by the new moon.
ev.loan_request.text.4: A neighbour asks to borrow for seed: last year's harvest rotted in the barn, and he has nothing to sow.
ev.loan_request.text.5: A neighbour asks for a loan for his eldest girl's wedding: without a dowry no one will take her, and time is running out.
ev.loan_request.text.6: A neighbour who's a craftsman asks to borrow money: all his tools were stolen, and without them he can't earn a thing.
ev.loan_request.text.7: The neighbour's only working animal died, and he's come to borrow for a new one. "Without it I can't feed my household."
ev.loan_request.text.8: A neighbour asks to borrow: his little one is burning with fever, and the healer won't come without payment.
ev.loan_request.text.9: A neighbour asks for a loan: an old relative of his has died, and he has nothing to give him a proper farewell with — and people will talk.
ev.loan_request.text.10: A neighbour is fired up about a new venture: buy goods in the next town and sell them on at a profit. All he's missing is money — yours.
ev.loan_request.text.11: The flood washed away half of the neighbour's yard and all his stores. He asks for a loan to tide him over to the next harvest and promises to repay with interest.
ev.loan_request.text.12: A neighbour has fallen into a moneylender's clutches, and the interest grows faster than he can work. He asks you for a loan — to pay the moneylender off and owe you instead, interest-free.
ev.loan_request.text.13: A neighbour asks to borrow so he can apprentice his boy to a good master: "Once he's trained, we'll pay it back three times over."
ev.loan_request.text.14: After the heavy rains a wall of a neighbour's house collapsed, and you can't live under the open sky with small children. He came to you first — he knows you have money put by.
ev.loan_request.text.15: A neighbour has been seized for debt and is held by his creditor until he pays. His eldest boy ran to you: "Lend it to us — he'll pay you back, I swear!"
ev.loan_request.text.16: The neighbour, always proud and taciturn, hovered at your gate for a long time before finally asking for a loan. He wouldn't say what had happened — only that without it he's done for.
ev.f_confession.text.1: At confession you admitted an old sin — a quarrel in which you were in the wrong, and the lie that grew out of it. The priest imposed a penance: forty days of fasting and prayer — and making peace.
ev.f_confession.text.2: At confession you admitted that you once kept something that wasn't yours and never gave it back. The priest ordered thirty days of fasting, morning prayers, and returning what you took — even if bit by bit.
ev.f_confession.text.3: You admitted to your confessor that you've nursed a grudge against a neighbour for years and wished him ill. The penance: fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays until the feast, and prostrations every evening.
ev.f_confession.text.4: At confession you repented of secretly eating meat during Lent. The priest sighed and imposed a penance: forty days of strict fasting and prayer — "so you learn to keep your word."
ev.f_confession.text.5: You admitted that you once swore falsely on a holy relic to win a dispute. The priest went pale and imposed a heavy penance: fasting, night vigils, and confessing to the one you deceived.
ev.f_confession.text.6: You repented of having struck, in anger, someone who couldn't strike back. Your confessor set a penance: fasting, prayers, and alms for the one you wronged — from your own hands.
ev.f_confession.text.7: At confession you admitted that you rejoice in others' misfortunes and envy their happiness. The priest told you to pray for forty days for the very people you envy, and to fast on Wednesdays.
ev.f_confession.text.8: You repented of not having attended a single service for over a year, apart from feast days. The priest imposed a penance: attend every morning service until Easter, and fast.
ev.f_confession.text.9: You admitted that, for gain, you cheated someone who trusted you. The priest imposed a penance: a month of fasting and prayer — and making it right with the one you cheated, down to the last coin.
ev.f_confession.text.10: You repented of spreading a vile rumour about a neighbour woman that turned the whole street against her. The priest prescribed forty days of fasting and prayer — and taking the words back in front of everyone.
ev.f_confession.text.11: At confession you recalled a debt you "forgot" to repay years ago because the lender died. The priest imposed a penance: fasting, prayers for his soul — and paying the debt to his heirs.
ev.f_confession.text.12: You admitted that you despise the poor and think yourself better than others. The priest, without looking up, set a penance: forty days of fasting and serving the beggars at the church with your own hands.
ev.f_confession.text.13: You repented of an old quarrel with a friend: you said too much, and you haven't spoken in years. The penance: fasting, prayer, and being the first to go and make peace.
ev.f_confession.text.14: You admitted that at the last feast you drank yourself senseless and said vile things to people. The priest imposed a penance: forty days without a drop, fasting, and asking forgiveness of each one.
ev.f_confession.text.15: You repented that once, in trouble, you vowed to go on pilgrimage — and when the trouble passed, the vow was forgotten. The priest told you to fulfil it now, and to fast and pray until you go.
ev.f_confession.text.16: Heavy thoughts kept you awake, and at last you went to confession and poured out everything that had built up over the years. The priest was silent a long time, then set a penance: forty days of fasting and prayer — and making peace with those you've wronged.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.1: They buried the neighbor you'd argued with for fifty years over the shared wall. Without his grumbling the street is far too quiet.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.2: They saw off the old potter you'd bought pots from all your life. The new pots are no worse — but somehow no better either.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.3: The old woman who sold flatbread on the corner for fifty years and knew everyone by name has died. Out of habit you turned toward her spot — and it was empty.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.4: The old friend you used to raid other people's orchards with as children has passed away. Now there's no one left to remember with you how you both got caught.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.5: The old storyteller whose tales you listened to as a child has died. At the farewell someone started telling one of them — and lost the thread halfway.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.6: They saw off the elder who had been settling the whole district's quarrels since you were young. Many people came, but you noticed how few of them were your own age.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.7: The neighbour who wished you good morning over the fence every day for fifty years has died. Mornings start far too quietly now.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.8: They saw off the old master you once learned some sense from — or he from you; you never did agree on which. He got the last word.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.9: Your old rival in every festival contest has died. For thirty years you matched each other in strength and wit, and only now do you realise how dear he was to you.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.10: They saw off the old water-carrier who'd brought water to your street for as long as you can remember. His jug still stands by the gate, and no one has the heart to take it.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.11: The old healer woman who treated all your childhood ailments has died. The whole district came to see her off — and almost every one of them had once lain under her cool compress.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.12: Another of your generation is gone — a quiet man you'd exchanged a few words with at the market for forty years. You suddenly realised you never learned his real name.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.13: They saw off the old singer who'd sung at every celebration in the district since you were a child. No one sang at his farewell: there was no voice fit for it.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.14: The neighbour you once paved the road to the river with has died. The road still stands, but of those who built it, only you remain.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.15: The old man who sat by the gate every evening scolding the young folk is gone. You sat down on his stone — and caught yourself grumbling exactly like him.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text.16: They saw off a man you'd once quarrelled with over a trifle and never made up with. At the farewell you couldn't even remember what it had been about.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.1: Before dawn you were sent out to the field with a clapper to chase the birds off the seed. By noon you were hoarse, but the crows seemed to respect you.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.2: You were handed a sling and told to guard the ripening grain from sparrows. Not a single sparrow was harmed, but you learned to throw a stone almost where you aim.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.3: You spent the whole day on a platform in the middle of the field, banging an old pot with a stick. The birds scattered, and people in the next fields shouted at you to bang more quietly.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.4: You made a scarecrow from an old shirt and dry grass and stood it proudly in the middle of the field. Next morning three crows were sitting on it — looking very pleased.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.5: You were set to guard the beds from birds, and you sang at the top of your lungs all day — that scares them off best, they say. The birds left. The neighbours looked like they'd have liked to, too.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.6: You ran round the field from morning to night waving a rag on a stick. By evening your legs were humming, but now you know every hummock and every boundary.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.7: You were sent to the field while it was still misty and told to clap whenever birds landed. By noon your palms were red, and you could tell one bird from another by its call.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.8: You were told to chase the birds off a freshly sown strip. You chased them so hard that by evening you fell asleep right on the boundary, clutching your clapper.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.9: A flock descended on the field all at once, like a cloud. You yelled, waved your arms and flung clods of earth until it lifted. The grown-ups said you'd done as well as any adult.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.10: You were posted at the edge of the field with a drum made from a hollowed gourd. You drummed all day, and by sunset the birds — and every dog in the neighbourhood — had decided to keep their distance.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.11: You guarded the field under the blazing sun, sheltering in the shade of the only bush. The birds soon caught on and landed at the far edge — so you ran back and forth until evening.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.12: A rope with potsherds tied along it was strung across the whole field: tug it and the sherds rattle and the birds fly up. You tugged until sunset and felt like the master of the field.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.13: For the first time you were left to guard the field alone, without the grown-ups. You were so afraid of letting them down that you didn't sit down once till evening — and not a single bird got away with a meal.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.14: You chased birds off the field in a fine drizzle, soaked to the skin. But by evening the old man from the next field showed you how to whistle so the whole flock takes off at once.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.15: You were set to guard the fields with the kids from the neighbouring farms. You divided them into patches and made a contest of it — and by evening yours was the cleanest patch, and yours the hoarsest throat.
ev.y_scare_birds.text.16: You spent the whole day in a little shelter at the edge of the field, leaping out with a yell whenever birds landed on the shoots. In the evening you were given an extra flatbread for your trouble.
